original_question: Let K be a compact subset of R^2 that meets every residue class modulo Z^2, and let A = (K-K) intersect Z^2. Which finite generating sets of Z^2 can arise in this way? In particular, can one realize the axis-cross set {(0,0),(±1,0),(0,±1)}?
target_in_paper: The draft targets the unnumbered problem in Section 2009.4.3 (Mel Nathanson) of the CANT notes: after the theorem that for a compact K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n meeting every congruence class mod \mathbb{Z}^n, the set A := (K-K) \cap \mathbb{Z}^n is finite and generates \mathbb{Z}^n, the paper asks for n=2 which generating sets arise in this fashion, specifically whether one can have A contained in the coordinate axes, and even more specifically whether A can equal {(0,0),(\pm1,0),(0,\pm1)}.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the ambient objects K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2 and A=(K-K)\cap\mathbb{Z}^2, the covering condition that K meets every residue class modulo \mathbb{Z}^2, the classification problem for which generating sets of \mathbb{Z}^2 can occur, and the highlighted special case of the axis-cross set {(0,0),(\pm1,0),(0,\pm1)}.
missing_details: The paper states the covering hypothesis explicitly as: for every x \in \mathbb{R}^n there exists y \in K with x-y \in \mathbb{Z}^n; in dimension 2 this should be written with x \in \mathbb{R}^2.
The notes first record the theorem that A=(K-K)\cap\mathbb{Z}^n is finite and generates the additive group \mathbb{Z}^n; this is part of the nearby context motivating the question.

The paper's n=2 problem includes an intermediate, stronger subquestion that your draft omits: whether there exists such a K for which A \subseteq \{(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2: xy=0\}, i.e. A lies entirely on the coordinate axes.
The phrase 'finite generating sets of \mathbb{Z}^2' should be understood as generating the additive group \mathbb{Z}^2.
To be fully stand-alone, the problem should state that K is compact in \mathbb{R}^2 and that A is defined from integer differences of points of K.
The official formulation in the notes is a question in the n=2 case, not a general conjecture with a complete characterization.
refined_question: Let K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2 be compact, and assume that K meets every congruence class modulo \mathbb{Z}^2; equivalently, for every x \in \mathbb{R}^2 there exists y \in K with x-y \in \mathbb{Z}^2. Define A := (K-K) \cap \mathbb{Z}^2. Since the nearby theorem states that such an A is a finite subset generating the additive group \mathbb{Z}^2, determine which finite generating sets A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^2 can arise in this way. More specifically, can one choose K so that A \subseteq \{(x,y) \in \mathbb{Z}^2 : xy=0\}? In particular, can one realize exactly the axis-cross set A = {(0,0),(\pm1,0),(0,\pm1)}?
justification: The draft is already close to the paper's intent, but the nearest official formulation in the cited paper is the unnumbered question in Section 2009.4.3, not a broader characterization problem from another source. The notes first define congruence mod \mathbb{Z}^n via differences in \mathbb{Z}^n, then state the theorem that A=(K-K)\cap\mathbb{Z}^n is finite and generates \mathbb{Z}^n, and only then ask, for n=2, which generating sets arise. The paper sharpens the special case in two stages: first asking whether A can be confined to the coordinate axes, and then whether the exact cross {(0,0),(\pm1,0),(0,\pm1)} can occur. Your draft captured the main objects and the final special case, but to be fully paper-faithful it should restore the explicit universal quantifier over x \in \mathbb{R}^2, mention the additive-group generation context from the preceding theorem, and retain the intermediate axis-support subquestion that appears in the official formulation.
